questions.q: White patches of oral thrush in the mouth of an AIDS patient are caused by:
questions.x: Oral thrush is an opportunistic infection by the yeast-like fungus Candida, which grows freely when cell-mediated immunity fails.

questions.q: Bacteriophage lambda can either destroy its host or join its DNA to the bacterial chromosome. It is therefore an example of a:
questions.x: A phage that can enter the lysogenic cycle is temperate; lambda is the standard example. A virulent phage such as T4 always follows the lytic cycle.

questions.q: Before beta-oxidation can begin, a fatty acid in the cytoplasm is first:
o: Activated by joining to coenzyme A, using energy from ATP
questions.x: A fatty acid is 'activated' by attaching to coenzyme A, a step that uses ATP; the fatty acyl CoA then enters the mitochondrion. Deamination applies to amino acids, not fats.

questions.q: Complete oxidation of one molecule of palmitic acid yields far more ATP than one molecule of glucose, mainly because palmitic acid:
o: Makes most of its ATP without oxygen
Has many more carbon and hydrogen atoms available for oxidation
Is respired entirely in the cytoplasm
questions.x: A 16-carbon fatty acid gives eight acetyl CoA plus many NADH and FADH2, all oxidized in the mitochondria. It does not pass through glycolysis at all.

questions.q: Ten glucose molecules (molecular mass 180 each) are joined into one unbranched chain. The molecular mass of water is 18. What is the molecular mass of the chain?
questions.x: Joining 10 units forms 9 glycosidic bonds, releasing 9 water molecules. Mass = 10 × 180 − 9 × 18 = 1800 − 162 = 1638.

questions.q: Which pair are both reducing sugars?
questions.x: All monosaccharides and the disaccharides maltose and lactose are reducing sugars. Every other pair contains sucrose, which is non-reducing.

questions.q: How many deoxyribose molecules are present in a double-stranded DNA segment of 500 base pairs?
questions.x: 500 base pairs contain 1000 nucleotides, and each nucleotide has one deoxyribose, so there are 1000 sugar molecules.

questions.q: Peptidoglycan (murein), the main component of bacterial cell walls, is made of:
o: Sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides
questions.x: Peptidoglycan is a conjugated molecule of polysaccharide chains linked by short chains of amino acids. Cellulose is found in plant cell walls and chitin in fungal walls.

questions.q: In a DNA nucleotide, the three components are linked in the order:
questions.x: The sugar is in the middle: the phosphate is attached to carbon 5 of deoxyribose and the base to carbon 1.

questions.q: Dietary fibre (roughage), which helps food move through the human intestine, is mainly:
questions.x: Humans cannot digest cellulose, so it passes through the gut as fibre and helps bowel movement. Glycogen, starch and sucrose are digested and absorbed as sugars.

questions.q: Which function is NOT normally carried out by proteins?
o: Storing hereditary information in most organisms
questions.x: Hereditary information is stored in DNA, a nucleic acid. Proteins act as enzymes, as carriers such as haemoglobin and as antibodies.

questions.q: The shape of a water molecule is:
questions.x: The two hydrogen atoms sit at an angle of about 104.5° on one side of the oxygen, so the molecule is bent. Because it is bent, the partial charges do not cancel and the molecule is polar.

questions.q: The backbone of each DNA strand consists of:
o: Base pairs joined by hydrogen bonds
A chain of deoxyribose molecules only
questions.x: Each strand's backbone is a repeating sugar–phosphate–sugar–phosphate chain. The bases stick out from the sugars towards the inside of the helix.

questions.q: A change in the nucleotide sequence of a gene is called a:
questions.x: Any change in the base sequence of a gene is a gene (point) mutation. Transcription, translation and replication are normal processes that copy or use the sequence.

questions.q: The reading frame in which an mRNA is translated is set by:
o: The position of the first stop codon
The position of the start codon AUG
The longest run of uracil bases
questions.x: Translation begins at the start codon, and every following triplet is read from that point, so AUG fixes the reading frame.

questions.q: If DNA had only three kinds of bases and codons were still triplets, how many different codons would be possible?
questions.x: With 3 choices for each of the 3 positions, there would be 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 codons. 64 = 4 × 4 × 4 is the number with the real four bases.

questions.q: The Golgi apparatus of plant cells synthesises wall polysaccharides that are not made at the plasma membrane. These are:
questions.x: Cellulose is made at the plasma membrane, but pectins and hemicelluloses are made in the Golgi and carried to the wall in vesicles.

questions.q: Alleles of a gene are found:
o: At different loci on the same chromosome
At the same locus on a pair of homologous chromosomes
questions.x: Alleles are alternative forms of one gene, such as tall and dwarf, and they sit at matching loci on the two homologous chromosomes.

questions.q: In prokaryotic cells, translation of an mRNA can begin while the mRNA is still being transcribed. This is possible because:
o: Prokaryotic mRNA is made in the nucleolus
There is no nuclear envelope separating DNA from ribosomes
questions.x: With no nuclear envelope, ribosomes can attach to an mRNA as soon as it starts to come off the DNA. In eukaryotes, mRNA must first leave the nucleus through nuclear pores.

questions.q: A girl's karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with only one X chromosome and no Y. She has:
questions.x: Turner syndrome is 45,X: a female with a single X chromosome. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY, and Down syndrome is trisomy 21.

questions.q: A person in a very cold room begins to shiver. The brain centre that detects the fall in blood temperature and starts shivering is the:
questions.x: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat: it senses blood temperature and triggers responses such as shivering. The thalamus relays sensory impulses to the cortex.

questions.q: During exercise, chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect a rise in blood carbon dioxide. The response that follows is:
o: A fall in both heart rate and breathing rate
An increase in the rate and depth of breathing
questions.x: Impulses from these chemoreceptors stimulate the breathing centre, so breathing becomes faster and deeper to remove the extra carbon dioxide.

questions.q: The grey matter of the brain and spinal cord consists mainly of:
o: Neuron cell bodies, dendrites and non-myelinated fibres
questions.x: Grey matter lacks much myelin; it is made of cell bodies, dendrites and non-myelinated fibres. White matter is mainly myelinated axons.

questions.q: The axon terminals of a motor neuron that supplies skeletal muscle end at:
o: Nodes of Ranvier on the muscle fibres
Neuromuscular junctions on the muscle fibres
questions.x: A motor neuron passes its signal to skeletal muscle at neuromuscular junctions. Nodes of Ranvier are features of myelinated axons, not muscle.

questions.q: Which type of neuron is the most numerous in the human nervous system?
questions.x: The vast majority of neurons lie entirely in the brain and spinal cord as associative neurons, linking and processing signals.

questions.q: The two properties most highly developed in neurons are:
questions.x: Neurons are specialised to respond to stimuli (excitability) and carry impulses (conductivity). Contractility is the special property of muscle.

questions.q: Which structure carries both the sensory and the motor fibres of a spinal reflex arc between the spinal cord and a limb?
o: The spinal nerve formed where the dorsal and ventral roots join
questions.x: The dorsal root carries only sensory fibres and the ventral root only motor fibres. They join to form the spinal nerve, which is a mixed nerve carrying both to and from the limb.

questions.q: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced mainly by the:
questions.x: Networks of capillaries called choroid plexuses, lining the ventricles, secrete cerebrospinal fluid. The dura mater is a protective membrane and the corpus callosum is a band of nerve fibres.

questions.q: Penicillin harms bacteria but not human cells mainly because:
o: Human cells have no cell wall, so they lack the enzyme it targets
questions.x: An inhibitor acts only on its target enzyme. The wall-building enzyme blocked by penicillin is not present in human cells.

questions.q: Vegetables are often dipped briefly in boiling water (blanched) before freezing. This is done to:
o: Denature the vegetables' own enzymes, which would otherwise slowly spoil them
Add extra enzymes to the vegetables
Raise the pH of the vegetables
questions.x: Freezing only slows enzymes, it does not destroy them. Brief heating denatures them so the food keeps its colour and taste longer.

questions.q: When lipase hydrolyses a fat, the other reactant used in the reaction is:
questions.x: Hydrolysis means splitting with water: water is added across each ester bond, giving glycerol and fatty acids.

questions.q: The rate of an enzyme reaction is measured as the:
o: Amount of product formed, or substrate used, per unit time
questions.x: Rate means how fast the reaction proceeds: how much product appears, or substrate disappears, in a given time.

questions.q: Carbonic anhydrase contains zinc ions that are essential for its activity. In this enzyme, zinc acts as:
questions.x: Metal ions such as Zn²⁺ that an enzyme needs to work are inorganic cofactors. A coenzyme is an organic cofactor, and the apoenzyme is the protein part.

questions.q: The germplasm theory was put forward by:
questions.x: Weismann proposed the germplasm theory, which says only the germ cells carry hereditary material to the next generation. It opposed Lamarck's idea.

questions.q: Dog breeders have docked (cut short) the tails of certain breeds for many generations, yet the puppies are still born with full tails. This supports the view of:
o: Weismann, that changes in body cells are not inherited
Lamarck, that acquired changes are inherited
Darwin, that the fittest leave more offspring
Oparin, that life arose from chemicals
questions.x: Cutting a tail changes only body (somatic) cells, not the germ cells, so the change is not passed on. This is just what Weismann's germplasm theory predicts.

questions.q: Which observation supports the idea that mitochondria evolved from bacteria living inside early cells?
o: Mitochondria are found only in plant cells
Mitochondria are made by the Golgi apparatus
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
questions.x: Like bacteria, mitochondria have circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and divide by a fission-like process. Chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts, not mitochondria.

questions.q: The middle piece of a human sperm is packed with mitochondria. Their role is to:
o: Supply ATP for the beating of the tail
Digest the coverings of the oocyte
Store food for the developing embryo
questions.x: Mitochondria in the middle piece produce ATP, which powers the movement of the flagellum. The chromosomes are in the head and the enzymes in the acrosome.

questions.q: The first menstruation in a girl's life, at puberty, is called:
questions.x: Menarche is the first menstrual period, usually at about 10 to 14 years of age. Menopause is the permanent end of the cycles.

questions.q: Spermatogonia, which lie next to the wall of the seminiferous tubule, increase in number by:
questions.x: Spermatogonia are diploid stem cells that multiply by mitosis. Some then grow into primary spermatocytes, which enter meiosis.

questions.q: The acrosome at the tip of the sperm head contains:
o: Mitochondria that supply energy for swimming
The centrioles that form the tail
Enzymes that help the sperm pass through the layers around the oocyte
questions.x: The acrosome is a cap of digestive enzymes, such as hyaluronidase, released to break through the coverings of the oocyte. Mitochondria lie in the middle piece.

questions.q: Which statement about the thick filaments of a relaxed sarcomere is correct?
o: They extend all the way from one Z line to the next
They are found only in the I band
They lie in the A band and do not reach the Z lines
They are attached at both ends to the Z lines
questions.x: Thick (myosin) filaments occupy the A band and are held at their centres by the M line; their ends stop short of the Z lines. The I band contains thin filaments only.

questions.q: By weight, about what proportion of bone matrix is made of inorganic mineral salts?
questions.x: Roughly two-thirds of bone matrix is inorganic (mainly calcium phosphate) and about one-third is organic (mainly collagen). One-third is the organic share, not the mineral share.

questions.q: Compared with aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration in a working muscle:
o: Gives far more ATP molecules per glucose
Gives far fewer ATP molecules per glucose
questions.x: Anaerobic respiration stops at lactic acid and yields only 2 ATP per glucose, far fewer than complete aerobic oxidation. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are made by yeast, not by human muscle.

questions.q: The largest synovial joint of the human body is the:
questions.x: The knee, between the femur, tibia and patella, is the largest synovial joint in the body. The elbow, wrist and ankle are all much smaller.

questions.q: Tendons are well suited to joining muscle to bone because they are:
o: Highly elastic, so they stretch and absorb most of the pull
Made of hyaline cartilage, so they reduce friction
Contractile, so they shorten together with the muscle
Strong and almost inelastic, so the pull of the muscle passes fully to the bone
questions.x: Tendons are dense bundles of collagen fibres: very strong and hardly stretchable, so the force of contraction is transmitted to the bone. They are not cartilage and cannot contract.

questions.q: Grouping joints as immovable, slightly movable and freely movable is a classification based on:
o: The size of the bones that meet
The number of bones in the joint
The amount of movement they allow
questions.x: This is the functional classification of joints, by degree of movement. It matches the structural types: fibrous joints are immovable, cartilaginous slightly movable and synovial freely movable.

questions.q: The muscles that move the eyeball in different directions are:
o: The same muscles that control the pupil
questions.x: The muscles attached to the outside of the eyeball are skeletal and under voluntary control. The muscles of the iris, which change pupil size, are smooth.

questions.q: An X-ray of a 10-year-old shows a plate of hyaline cartilage joining the shaft of a long bone to its end. This is a temporary joint of which type?
questions.x: The growth (epiphyseal) plate joins two parts of a bone by cartilage with no cavity, so it is a cartilaginous joint; it turns to bone when growth ends. It has no synovial fluid and no fibrous tissue joining the parts.

questions.q: In a dihybrid F2 (RrYy selfed), the round yellow class is made up of how many distinct genotypes?
questions.x: Round yellow plants can be RRYY, RRYy, RrYY or RrYy, which is four genotypes. Nine is the total number of genotypes in the whole F2.

questions.q: The X and Y chromosomes, which differ between the sexes, are also called:
questions.x: Sex chromosomes are also called allosomes or heterosomes. Autosomes are the chromosomes that are the same in both sexes.

questions.q: For an X-linked recessive allele to show its effect in a woman, she must be:
o: Carrying the allele on her Y chromosome
questions.x: A woman has two X chromosomes, so the recessive allele shows only when both X chromosomes carry it. A heterozygous woman is a carrier with normal phenotype.

questions.q: The chromosome set of a normal human female body cell is:
questions.x: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes: 44 autosomes and two sex chromosomes, XX in females. 22 + X is the set in an egg.

questions.q: In a family tree, which observation would rule out X-linked recessive inheritance of a trait?
o: An affected woman has a son with the normal phenotype
An affected man has unaffected parents
An affected man has only unaffected sons
Two unaffected parents have an affected son
questions.x: An affected woman has the allele on both X chromosomes, so every son must receive it and be affected. A normal son of hers rules out X-linked recessive inheritance.

questions.q: For an autosomal recessive condition, a couple are both heterozygous (Aa). What is the chance that their first child is unaffected and their second child is affected?
questions.x: Each birth is independent. P(unaffected) = 3/4 and P(affected) = 1/4, so the chance of this order is 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16.

questions.q: Contrasting forms of one character, such as round and wrinkled seed shape, are called:
questions.x: A character (seed shape) has contrasting traits (round, wrinkled). A locus is a gene's position, a genome is the full set of genes, and a linkage group is the genes on one chromosome.

questions.q: In Mendel's classic example of independent assortment in peas, the two characters followed together were:
questions.x: Mendel's well-known dihybrid cross was round yellow × wrinkled green seeds, so the characters were seed shape and seed colour.

questions.q: While the whole heart is relaxed, blood flows into the atria from the:
questions.x: During complete diastole the atria fill from the veins: venae cavae on the right and pulmonary veins on the left. The aorta and pulmonary trunk carry blood away from the heart.

questions.q: The largest lymphoid organ of the human body is the:
questions.x: The spleen is the largest single mass of lymphoid tissue. The thymus, tonsils and appendix are much smaller.

questions.q: Backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle is prevented by the:
questions.x: The aortic semilunar valve lies at the base of the aorta. The bicuspid valve guards the left atrium–ventricle opening, and the pulmonary semilunar valve guards the pulmonary trunk.

questions.q: If the SA node stops working, the heart usually:
o: Stops beating at once and cannot restart
Keeps beating, but more slowly, under the control of the AV node
Beats faster because the vagus nerve takes over
questions.x: Other conducting tissue, especially the AV node, can produce impulses on its own but at a slower rate. So the heart continues beating slowly; nerves only change the rate, they do not start the beat.

questions.q: Anaphylactic shock is:
o: A mild skin rash that fades in minutes
A sudden, severe allergic reaction affecting the whole body that can be life-threatening
questions.x: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, whole-body allergic reaction, for example to a bee sting or a drug. Blood pressure can fall and breathing become difficult, so it is a medical emergency.

questions.q: Antibodies in the plasma cannot reach a virus once it is inside a body cell. The infection is then controlled mainly by:
o: Plasma cells entering the infected cells
Red blood cells absorbing the virus
Cytotoxic T cells destroying the infected cells
Memory B cells digesting the virus
questions.x: Viruses inside cells are hidden from antibodies. Cytotoxic T cells recognise viral antigens displayed on the infected cell's surface and kill the cell, stopping the virus from multiplying.

questions.q: A stab wound lets outside air enter the pleural cavity on one side of the chest. The lung on that side collapses because:
o: Its alveoli fill with blood and can no longer hold air
The diaphragm on that side stops receiving nerve impulses
The pressure around it is no longer lower than the pressure inside it, so its elastic tissue recoils
The trachea is pushed shut by the air in the wound
questions.x: Normally the pleural pressure is below the pressure in the lungs, which keeps the elastic lungs stretched against the chest wall. When air enters the pleural cavity this pressure difference is lost and the lung recoils and collapses.

questions.q: Breathing movements (ventilation) help gas exchange in the alveoli mainly by:
o: Pumping oxygen directly into the blood
Making the alveolar walls more permeable
Keeping the oxygen level high and the carbon dioxide level low in alveolar air
Raising the temperature of alveolar air
questions.x: Ventilation constantly brings in fresh air and removes stale air, so oxygen in the alveoli stays higher and carbon dioxide lower than in the blood. This maintains the gradients for diffusion.

questions.q: Nicotine acts on the nervous system by:
o: Binding to acetylcholine receptors at synapses
Blocking the release of all neurotransmitters
Destroying the myelin sheath of neurons
Replacing sodium ions in the axon membrane
questions.x: Nicotine has a shape similar to acetylcholine and binds to its receptors on postsynaptic membranes, stimulating them. This action in the brain's reward pathways is linked to its addictive effect.

questions.q: Continuous flow of blood through the capillaries around the alveoli helps gas exchange because it:
o: Pushes oxygen actively into the red blood cells
Carries oxygenated blood away, keeping a steep oxygen gradient
Adds carbon dioxide to the alveolar air by active transport
questions.x: As fresh deoxygenated blood keeps arriving and oxygenated blood keeps leaving, the oxygen level in the capillary stays lower than in the alveolus, so diffusion continues. No active transport is involved.

questions.q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, excess glucose reaching the liver is stored there as:
questions.x: The liver converts excess glucose into glycogen, the animal storage polysaccharide, and breaks it down again when blood glucose falls. Starch and cellulose are plant polysaccharides.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a role of the tongue in the mouth?
o: Rolling chewed food into a bolus
Pushing the bolus back into the pharynx
questions.x: The muscular tongue mixes food with saliva, shapes it into a bolus, pushes it back for swallowing and carries taste buds. Salivary amylase is made by the salivary glands, not the tongue.

questions.q: Which statement about where the two capillary beds of a nephron lie is correct?
o: Both beds lie only in the medulla
Glomerular capillaries lie in the medulla; peritubular capillaries only in the cortex
Both beds lie in the renal pelvis
Glomerular capillaries lie only in the cortex; peritubular capillaries lie in the cortex and, as vasa recta, in the medulla
questions.x: All glomeruli are in the cortex. Peritubular capillaries surround the convoluted tubules in the cortex, and their vasa recta branches dip into the medulla alongside the loops.

questions.q: Besides calcium oxalate, calcium-containing kidney stones can also be made of:
questions.x: Calcium stones are of calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate. The other salts are soluble and do not form common kidney stones.

questions.q: Severe dehydration from cholera or prolonged diarrhoea can cause acute kidney failure because:
o: Cholera bacteria grow inside the nephrons
Diarrhoea fluid flows back into the ureters
Blood volume falls, so too little blood reaches the kidneys to be filtered
The kidneys reabsorb too much glucose
questions.x: Heavy fluid loss lowers blood volume and pressure, so filtration in the glomeruli falls and the kidney tissue is starved of blood.

questions.q: Medicines that make the urine less acidic can slowly dissolve which type of kidney stone?
questions.x: Uric acid is much more soluble in less acidic urine, so these stones can dissolve. Calcium phosphate and struvite stones actually form more easily in alkaline urine.

questions.q: The last part of the nephron itself, which joins a collecting duct, is the:
questions.x: The nephron runs Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, then DCT. The DCT empties into a collecting duct, which is shared by several nephrons.

questions.q: In a person with liver disease, the level of plasma proteins is low. If other conditions stay the same, glomerular filtration would:
o: Increase, because the osmotic pressure opposing filtration is lower
Decrease, because there is less protein to push fluid out
Stop, because proteins are needed to carry water
Stay the same, because proteins are not filtered
questions.x: Plasma proteins create an osmotic pressure that holds water in the glomerular blood and opposes filtration. With fewer proteins this opposing force falls, so net filtration pressure and filtration rise.

questions.q: In composition, glomerular filtrate is essentially:
o: Blood plasma without its plasma proteins
Whole blood without its red blood cells
Urine that has not yet lost its urea
questions.x: Filtrate contains water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea at plasma concentrations, but blood cells and plasma proteins are too large to pass. Its composition is then changed along the tubule to make urine.

questions.q: If the efferent arteriole were as wide as the afferent arteriole, the most direct effect would be that:
o: Glomerular blood pressure and filtration would fall
Plasma proteins would enter the filtrate
Pressure in the peritubular capillaries would fall to zero
questions.x: The narrower outflow is what keeps glomerular pressure high. Without it blood would leave freely, glomerular pressure would drop, and less filtrate would form.

questions.q: Where along the nephron does reabsorption take place?
o: Only in the loop of Henle
Along the whole tubule, from PCT to collecting duct, though mostly in the PCT
Only in the collecting duct, under ADH
questions.x: Every part of the tubule reabsorbs something: most solutes and water in the PCT, water and salts in the loop, and controlled amounts in the DCT and collecting duct. The glomerulus only filters.

questions.q: Home ovulation-prediction kits use monoclonal antibodies to detect a rise in the urine level of:
questions.x: A surge of LH triggers ovulation, so detecting it in urine shows that ovulation is about to occur. hCG is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.

questions.q: In Southern blotting, DNA fragments separated by gel electrophoresis are transferred to a membrane and then:
o: Tested with a labelled probe to find a particular sequence
questions.x: Blotting fixes the separated fragments on a membrane; a labelled probe then shows which band contains the target sequence. Ligase joins DNA rather than cutting it.

questions.q: Recombinant factor VIII and erythropoietin are usually produced in cultured mammalian cells rather than in bacteria because:
o: These proteins need modifications, such as added sugar groups, that bacteria cannot carry out
Mammalian cells multiply faster than bacteria
These proteins are poisonous to all bacteria
questions.x: Many human proteins work properly only after processing such as glycosylation, which bacteria lack. Mammalian cells, for example hamster ovary cells, process them like human cells, though they grow more slowly than bacteria.

questions.q: For large-scale production of a recombinant vaccine protein, the genetically modified yeast cells are grown in:
questions.x: Fermenters provide the right temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrients so the engineered microbes multiply and make the protein in large amounts. Eggs are used for growing viruses, not yeast.

questions.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, a vessel contains 2 mol of N₂ and 9 mol of H₂. Which statement is correct?
o: H₂ is limiting, because there is less H₂ than needed
N₂ is limiting, because 2 mol N₂ needs only 6 mol H₂
H₂ is limiting, because 9 mol H₂ needs 3 mol N₂
Neither is limiting, because they are in the exact ratio
questions.x: 2 mol N₂ needs 3 × 2 = 6 mol H₂, and 9 mol is available, so H₂ is in excess and N₂ runs out first. 9 mol H₂ would need 3 mol N₂, but only 2 mol is present.

questions.q: Magnesium dissolves in acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What mass of magnesium gives 1.12 dm³ of hydrogen at STP? (Mg = 24)
questions.x: Moles of H₂ = 1.12/22.4 = 0.05 mol; ratio Mg : H₂ = 1 : 1, so 0.05 mol Mg = 0.05 × 24 = 1.2 g. 0.6 g wrongly applies the 2 : 1 ratio meant for HCl.

questions.q: Compared with cathode rays in the same magnetic field, positive rays are deflected:
o: More, and in the opposite direction
Less, and in the same direction
Less, and in the opposite direction
More, and in the same direction
questions.x: Positive ions are far heavier than electrons, so they bend much less; their charge is opposite, so they bend the opposite way.

questions.q: An orbital can hold at most two electrons. This limit follows directly from:
questions.x: Electrons in one orbital share n, l and m, so by Pauli they must differ in spin. Only two spin values exist, so at most two electrons fit.

questions.q: The German word Aufbau, used for the rule of filling orbitals, means:
questions.x: Aufbau means building up: electrons are added one by one into orbitals of increasing energy.

questions.q: In the van der Waals equation, the term added to the measured pressure P to correct for intermolecular attractions is:
questions.x: The equation is (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT. The term an²/V² corrects pressure for attractions, and nb corrects volume for the size of the molecules.

questions.q: What is the mass of 2.24 dm³ of sulphur dioxide, SO₂, at STP? (S = 32, O = 16)
questions.x: 2.24 dm³ at STP is 0.1 mol; M(SO₂) = 32 + 32 = 64 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.1 × 64 = 6.4 g.

questions.q: 4.4 g of a gas occupies 1.12 dm³ at 2 atm and 273 K. What is its molar mass? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 0.0821 × 273 ≈ 22.4)
questions.x: M = mRT/PV = (4.4 × 22.4)/(2 × 1.12) = 98.56/2.24 = 44 g mol⁻¹. Leaving out the pressure gives the wrong 88.

questions.q: While a pure liquid is boiling at constant external pressure, its temperature:
o: Stays constant, as the heat supplied is used to overcome intermolecular forces
Keeps rising steadily until all the liquid has boiled
Falls, because the fastest molecules escape
questions.x: During boiling, the heat supplied (latent heat of vaporisation) separates molecules against their attractions instead of raising the temperature.

questions.q: An ice cube (density 0.92 g cm⁻³) floats in water (density 1.00 g cm⁻³). The fraction of its volume below the water surface is about:
questions.x: A floating object sinks until it displaces its own mass of water, so fraction submerged = 0.92/1.00 = 92%. Only about 8% stays above the surface.

questions.q: An ionic compound has a radius ratio between 0.155 and 0.225. The expected coordination number of the cation is:
questions.x: A radius ratio of 0.155–0.225 gives a triangular arrangement with coordination number 3. Coordination number 4 needs 0.225–0.414.

questions.q: When lattice energy is defined as the energy change on forming one mole of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions, its value is always:
o: Positive for small ions and negative for large ions
questions.x: Bringing oppositely charged gaseous ions together into a lattice releases energy, so this lattice energy is exothermic (negative).

questions.q: A CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa buffer is diluted with an equal volume of water. Its pH:
o: Falls sharply, because the acid becomes stronger
Rises to 7, because water is neutral
Halves, because both concentrations are halved
Stays almost the same, because the ratio [salt]/[acid] is unchanged
questions.x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]); dilution halves both concentrations, so the ratio and hence the pH hardly change.

questions.q: A weak acid HX has pKa = 5.0. A buffer contains 0.2 mol dm⁻³ HX and 0.02 mol dm⁻³ NaX. Its pH is:
questions.x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 5.0 + log(0.02/0.2) = 5.0 + log(0.1) = 5.0 − 1 = 4.0. Inverting the ratio gives 6.0.

questions.q: The units of the rate constant k of a reaction depend on:
o: The enthalpy change of the reaction
The overall order of the reaction
The value of the activation energy
The initial concentration of the reactants
questions.x: Rate always has units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, so the units of k must change with the overall order to balance the concentration terms.

questions.q: For rate = k[X]²[Y], the concentration of X is halved and the concentration of Y is doubled. The rate becomes:
o: The same as the original rate
One quarter of the original rate
questions.x: New rate factor = (½)² × 2 = ¼ × 2 = ½. Forgetting to square the X term would wrongly give no change.

questions.q: Once formed, an activated complex can:
o: Only go back to the reactants
Either break up into products or go back to the reactants
Be collected and stored as a stable compound
questions.x: The activated complex is very unstable and decomposes at once, either forward to products or back to reactants.

questions.q: A candle does not burn until it is lit, but once lit it keeps burning by itself. Which statement is correct?
o: Burning is non-spontaneous because the candle had to be lit
Burning is endothermic, so it needs the match all the time
Burning is spontaneous only while the match is held to it
Burning is spontaneous; lighting only supplies the energy needed to start it
questions.x: Some spontaneous reactions need initiation. The match supplies the activation energy; after that, the reaction continues on its own.

questions.q: A machine that does work forever without taking energy from any source (a perpetual motion machine of the first kind) is impossible because it would:
o: Need a catalyst that is used up
Have to work at constant volume
Need an activation energy of zero
Create energy, against the first law of thermodynamics
questions.x: The first law says energy cannot be created; work out without energy in would create energy.

questions.q: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. The standard emf of a cell made from these two electrodes is:
questions.x: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Doubling the silver value to 1.60 (giving 2.36) is wrong, since E° does not depend on coefficients.

questions.q: A cell reaction is feasible (spontaneous) under standard conditions when the standard emf of the cell, E°cell, is:
o: Equal to the E° of the SHE
questions.x: A positive E°cell means the reaction as written proceeds spontaneously; a negative value means the reverse reaction is the spontaneous one.

questions.q: The H–N–H bond angle in NH₄⁺ (109.5°) is larger than in NH₃ (107°) because in NH₄⁺:
o: Nitrogen has two lone pairs instead of one
The lone pair of nitrogen has become a bond pair
questions.x: When NH₃ accepts H⁺, its lone pair forms the fourth N–H bond. Four equal bond pairs give a regular tetrahedron of 109.5°, with no extra lone-pair repulsion.

questions.q: The observed dipole moment of HBr is 0.80 D. The dipole moment calculated for HBr as a 100% ionic compound is 5.0 D. The percentage ionic character of the H–Br bond is:
questions.x: % ionic character = (0.80 / 5.0) × 100 = 16%. 84% is the covalent part, and 62.5% comes from dividing the wrong way round.

questions.q: Silane, SiH₄, has four bond pairs and no lone pair around silicon. The H–Si–H bond angle is about:
questions.x: Four bond pairs with no lone pair arrange themselves tetrahedrally, giving 109.5°. 107° would need one lone pair, as in NH₃.

questions.q: 4.6 g of sodium reacts completely with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. What mass of sodium hydroxide is formed? (Na 23, O 16, H 1)
questions.x: Moles of Na = 4.6/23 = 0.2; the ratio Na : NaOH is 1 : 1, so 0.2 × 40 = 8.0 g NaOH. Halving the moles gives the wrong 4.0 g.

questions.q: Removing one electron from a gaseous N atom needs more energy than removing one from a gaseous O atom. Why?
o: Nitrogen has a larger nuclear charge than oxygen
Oxygen's outer electron is in a higher shell
Nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p subshell, while oxygen's paired 2p electron is repelled and easier to remove
Nitrogen atoms are larger than oxygen atoms
questions.x: N is 2p³ (half-filled, each orbital singly occupied). In O (2p⁴) one orbital holds a pair, and repulsion makes one of those electrons easier to remove.

questions.q: A ground-state nickel atom (Ni, Z = 28) has how many unpaired electrons?
questions.x: Ni is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². The 4s pair is full; in 3d⁸ three orbitals are paired and two hold single electrons, giving 2 unpaired.

questions.q: The functional group present in alcohols is:
questions.x: Alcohols, such as ethanol CH₃CH₂OH, contain an –OH group bonded to a saturated carbon atom.

questions.q: Which of the following is a substitution reaction?
o: Benzene with hydrogen over heated nickel
Methylbenzene with chlorine in bright sunlight at its boiling point
questions.x: In sunlight, chlorine replaces a hydrogen of the –CH₃ side chain to give C₆H₅CH₂Cl and HCl. The other three reactions add atoms across multiple bonds.

questions.q: 2,2,3,3-tetrabromobutane, CH₃CBr₂CBr₂CH₃, is heated with zinc dust. The organic product is:
questions.x: Zinc removes all four bromine atoms (as ZnBr₂) from the two central carbons, leaving a triple bond between C2 and C3.

questions.q: Which general statement about resonance and stability is correct?
o: A molecule with more equivalent contributing structures generally gains more resonance stabilisation
A molecule with more contributing structures is always less stable
Resonance makes a molecule higher in energy than its contributing structures
Resonance stabilisation is possible only for ions, not molecules
questions.x: Spreading electrons over more equivalent structures lowers the energy of the hybrid, increasing stability. Resonance occurs in molecules such as benzene as well as in ions.

questions.q: Hexane and its chain isomers all share the formula C₆H₁₄. Including hexane itself, the total number of such isomers is:
questions.x: They are hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane: five in all.

questions.q: A symmetrical six-carbon alkene, CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₂CH₃, is named by IUPAC as:
questions.x: The six-carbon chain has its double bond between carbons 3 and 4 from either end, so it is hex-3-ene.

questions.q: When three hydrogen atoms of methane are replaced by chlorine, the product is:
questions.x: Replacing three H atoms of CH₄ gives CHCl₃, trichloromethane, commonly called chloroform. CCl₄ results when all four are replaced.

questions.q: The C–C σ bonds that hold the benzene ring together are formed by overlap of:
o: sp² orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
Unhybridised p orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
sp³ orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
sp orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms
questions.x: Each ring carbon is sp² hybridised and uses two sp² orbitals for head-on overlap with its two neighbours. The unhybridised p orbitals form the delocalised π system.

questions.q: An alkyl halide is hydrolysed by the SN1 mechanism. If [RX] is tripled and [OH⁻] is doubled at the same time, the rate becomes:
questions.x: For SN1, rate = k[RX], so only the alkyl halide concentration matters and the rate rises 3 times. Six times wrongly includes the [OH⁻] term.

questions.q: Bromoethane heated with concentrated alcoholic KOH loses HBr mainly by which mechanism?
questions.x: Bromoethane is primary, and a primary carbocation is too unstable for E1, so the strong base removes H while Br leaves in one step (E2). SN1 and SN2 are substitutions, not loss of HBr.

questions.q: In water, ethanol is neutral, while phenol is:
questions.x: Phenol ionises slightly to give phenoxide and H⁺, so it is a weak acid (carbolic acid). Ethanol ionises even less than water and is regarded as neutral.

questions.q: Phenol vapour is passed over heated zinc dust. The organic product is:
questions.x: Zinc dust removes the oxygen: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO. This reduction converts phenol back into benzene.

questions.q: Aldehydes behave as reducing agents because they:
o: Are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids
questions.x: A reducing agent is itself oxidised. The H on the aldehyde carbonyl carbon lets aldehydes be oxidised readily to acids, so they reduce Ag⁺ and Cu²⁺.

questions.q: 6.0 g of propan-1-ol (M = 60) is oxidised and 4.35 g of propanal (M = 58) is collected. What is the percentage yield? (1 mol alcohol gives 1 mol aldehyde)
questions.x: 0.1 mol propan-1-ol gives at most 0.1 mol × 58 = 5.8 g propanal. Yield = 4.35/5.8 × 100 = 75%. 72.5% wrongly compares 4.35 g with the 6.0 g of alcohol.

questions.q: Which Grignard reagent, after reaction with carbon dioxide and hydrolysis with dilute acid, gives propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH?
questions.x: The CO₂ adds one carbon as –COOH, so a two-carbon (ethyl) Grignard gives the three-carbon acid. CH₃MgBr would give ethanoic acid.

questions.q: The ester CH₃COOCH₃ is named:
questions.x: The alkyl group from the alcohol (methyl) is named first, then the acid part (ethanoate, from CH₃COO–).

questions.q: Which enzyme, substrate and product match is correct?
questions.x: Maltase hydrolyses maltose into two glucose units. Glucose to ethanol is done by zymase, and urease gives ammonia and carbon dioxide from urea.

questions.q: Which polymer is a homopolymer, made from a single kind of monomer?
questions.x: PVC is made only from chloroethene. Nylon-6,6 (diamine and diacid), Terylene (diol and diacid) and Bakelite (phenol and methanal) each need two different monomers.

questions.q: A force F = (4î + 3ĵ) N moves a body through a displacement d = (5î) m. The work done by the force is:
questions.x: W = F · d = (4)(5) + (3)(0) = 20 J. Only the component of force along the displacement does work; 25 J wrongly uses the full 5 N magnitude.

questions.q: A ball's kinetic energy is E when it is launched at 60° to the horizontal. With no air drag, how much kinetic energy does it have at the top of its path? (cos 60° = 0.5)
questions.x: At the top only the horizontal component v cos 60° = v/2 remains. KE = ½m(v/2)² = ¼ × ½mv² = E/4. E/2 forgets to square the factor ½.

questions.q: A particle on the x-axis is at x = 2 m at t = 0 and at x = 14 m at t = 4 s. Its average velocity over this interval is:
questions.x: Average velocity = (14 − 2) m ÷ 4 s = 3 m s⁻¹. 3.5 m s⁻¹ wrongly uses the final position 14 m instead of the change in position.

questions.q: Ball P moving at 5 m s⁻¹ meets ball Q moving at 3 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. They collide head-on, perfectly elastically, and Q then moves at 4 m s⁻¹ in P's original direction. The velocity of P afterwards is:
o: 4 m s⁻¹ in its original direction
questions.x: Relative speed of approach = 5 + 3 = 8 m s⁻¹, which must equal the speed of separation: 4 − v(P) = 8, so v(P) = −4 m s⁻¹, i.e. 4 m s⁻¹ reversed.

questions.q: A particle moves in a plane from the point (1 m, 2 m) to the point (4 m, 6 m). The magnitude of its displacement is:
questions.x: Change in x = 3 m and change in y = 4 m, so displacement = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m. 7 m simply adds the two changes.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, which statement about a projectile launched at an angle is NOT correct?
o: Its horizontal velocity decreases as it rises
Its vertical acceleration is g downward
Its vertical velocity is zero at the highest point
questions.x: The horizontal velocity stays constant, because no horizontal force acts. The other three statements are true.

questions.q: Plotting x (horizontal distance travelled) of a projectile against time gives, when air drag is negligible:
o: A straight line through the origin
A curve that becomes flatter with time
questions.x: Horizontal velocity is constant, so x = (v cos θ)t, which is a straight line through the origin with slope v cos θ.

questions.q: The work done by a constant force on a moving body is negative when the angle θ between the force and the displacement lies in the range:
questions.x: W = Fd cos θ is negative when cos θ is negative, i.e. for angles greater than 90° up to 180°. At exactly 90° the work is zero.

questions.q: Work is done on a body by a force only when:
o: The force acts on the body, whether or not the body moves
The body moves at constant velocity with no force acting on it
The force always acts at right angles to the motion
The body is displaced and the displacement has a component along the force
questions.x: W = Fd cos θ, so work needs a displacement with a component along the force. A force with no displacement, or one at 90° to the motion, does no work.

questions.q: Through what angle does the second hand of a clock turn in 15 seconds?
questions.x: The second hand makes one revolution (2π rad) in 60 s, so in 15 s it turns 15/60 × 2π = π/2 rad.

questions.q: The angular speed of the second hand of a clock is:
questions.x: The second hand turns 2π rad in 60 s, so ω = 2π/60 = π/30 rad s⁻¹.

questions.q: A pipe of area 6 cm² carries water at 2 m s⁻¹. It divides into three branches: two have area 1 cm² and carry water at 3 m s⁻¹ each, and the third has area 2 cm². The speed of the water in the third branch is:
questions.x: Flow in = 6 × 2 = 12 (cm² m s⁻¹). The two small branches carry 2 × 1 × 3 = 6, leaving 6 for the third: v = 6 / 2 = 3 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: Air drag on a car at motorway speed is mainly due to turbulent flow. If the car's speed is doubled, the drag force on it:
o: Increases to more than twice its value
questions.x: In laminar (Stokes) conditions drag is proportional to speed, but in turbulent conditions it rises much faster, roughly with the square of the speed, so doubling speed gives much more than twice the drag.

questions.q: Two tiny balls are pulled at one common, slow speed through syrup. One ball has three times the radius of the other. The drag (F = 6πηrv) on the larger ball is:
questions.x: Stokes' law F = 6πηrv shows F ∝ r at a fixed speed, so tripling r triples the drag. The r² dependence belongs to terminal velocity, not to the drag formula.

questions.q: A wave's energy varies as the square of its amplitude. By what factor must the amplitude increase for the wave to deliver 9 times the energy, with frequency unchanged?
questions.x: Energy ∝ A², so the amplitude must increase by √9 = 3. A factor of 9 in amplitude would give 81 times the energy.

questions.q: A wave has a speed of 300 m s⁻¹ and a frequency of 100 Hz. Its wavelength is:
questions.x: λ = v/f = 300/100 = 3 m. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 30 000 m.

questions.q: As a progressive wave passes, which quantity for a particular particle of the medium keeps changing with time, while its amplitude stays constant?
o: The time period of its vibration
questions.x: Displacement is the particle's distance from its mean position at a given instant, so it changes continuously between +A and −A. Amplitude is the fixed maximum value of that displacement.

questions.q: Which of the following can travel through a vacuum?
questions.x: X-rays are electromagnetic waves and need no medium. Sound, water waves and string waves are mechanical waves and need a material medium.

questions.q: According to the principle of superposition, when two waves meet at a point, the quantity that is added, taking signs into account, is:
questions.x: Superposition adds the displacements of the individual waves at each instant. Intensities and energies are not simply added, which is why destructive interference can occur.

questions.q: An organ builder wants a stopped pipe (closed at one end) to give the same lowest note as an open pipe 1.2 m long. Ignoring end correction, the stopped pipe should be:
questions.x: Open pipe: f = v/2L = v/2.4. Closed pipe: f = v/4L'. Setting them equal gives 4L' = 2.4 m, so L' = 0.6 m.

questions.q: A 100 W immersion heater heats 0.5 kg of a liquid for 2 minutes and its temperature rises by 6 K. Ignoring losses, the specific heat of the liquid is:
questions.x: Heat = power × time = 100 × 120 = 12 000 J. c = Q ÷ mΔT = 12 000 ÷ (0.5 × 6) = 4000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Using 2 s instead of 120 s gives about 67.

questions.q: When an ideal gas is heated at constant volume, the heat supplied goes:
o: Entirely into doing work on the surroundings
Entirely into increasing its internal energy
Partly into internal energy and partly into work
Nowhere, because the temperature cannot change
questions.x: At constant volume ΔV = 0, so the gas does no work. All the heat (nCvΔT) raises its internal energy and so its temperature.

questions.q: On a pressure–volume graph, a change of a gas is shown by a vertical straight line. The work done by the gas in this change is:
o: Equal to P × V at the top of the line
Equal to the length of the line
questions.x: A vertical line means the volume does not change (only the pressure does). With ΔV = 0 the area under the line is zero, so no work is done.

questions.q: In Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r² for charges in free space, the constant k = 1/4πε₀ has the value:
questions.x: k = 1/4πε₀ ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². 8.85 × 10⁻¹² is ε₀ itself and 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ is the gravitational constant.

questions.q: Point charges +3 nC and −1 nC are fixed 2 m from each other. Halfway between them, V equals: (take k as 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
questions.x: Potential is a scalar, so add with signs: V = k(3 × 10⁻⁹ − 1 × 10⁻⁹)/1 = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹ = 18 V. Ignoring the minus sign gives 36 V.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged from a 10 V battery through a resistor. After one time constant, the capacitor's voltage is about 6.3 V. The voltage across the resistor at that moment is about:
questions.x: In the series loop the battery voltage is shared: V_R = 10 − 6.3 = 3.7 V. The resistor voltage (and so the current) falls as the capacitor voltage rises.

questions.q: Power stations and large batteries are not usually run under the maximum power transfer condition because:
o: The efficiency would be only 50%, so half the energy would be wasted in the source
The load would receive no power at all
The emf of the source would double
questions.x: At R = r equal power is lost inside the source and delivered to the load, so efficiency is only 50%. Where efficiency matters, R is made much larger than r.

questions.q: In a pure semiconductor such as silicon, the electric current is carried by:
questions.x: In a semiconductor, freed electrons move one way and the holes they leave behind move the other way; both carry current. Ions carry current in electrolytes.

questions.q: A current-carrying wire at right angles to a uniform field feels a force of 0.8 N. It is turned so that it makes 30° with the field, with the same current. The force becomes (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87):
questions.x: F = ILB sin θ. At 90° it is 0.8 N; at 30° it is 0.8 × sin 30° = 0.4 N. Using cos 30° gives about 0.7 N, which is wrong.

questions.q: A transmission line of resistance 4 Ω carries a current of 25 A. The voltage lost along the line is:
questions.x: Voltage drop = IR = 25 × 4 = 100 V. Higher transmission voltage means less current, so less voltage is lost along the line.

questions.q: Find the output voltage of an ideal step-down transformer with turns ratio Np : Ns = 20 : 1, fed from 220 V AC.
questions.x: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 220 × 1/20 = 11 V. Inverting the ratio gives 4400 V.

questions.q: A coil of inductance (0.2/π) H and negligible resistance is used on a 50 Hz supply. Its reactance XL = 2πfL is:
Pure silicon is doped with a pentavalent impurity such as arsenic. The majority charge carriers in the resulting material are:
questions.x: Each pentavalent atom has one spare valence electron, giving n-type material in which free electrons are the majority carriers.

questions.q: Hydrogen atoms excited to the fourth energy level fall back to the ground state by every possible route. The total number of distinct spectral lines possible is:
questions.x: Number of lines = n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6: transitions 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1.

questions.q: Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) decays by emitting a beta particle (an electron). The daughter nucleus is:
questions.x: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton: A stays 14 and Z rises from 6 to 7, giving nitrogen-14.

questions.q: An isotope's half-life is 1386 s. What is its decay constant?
questions.x: λ = 0.693/1386 = 0.0005 = 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Inverting the ratio gives 2 × 10³, which is wrong.

questions.q: Sometimes I still walk past the school where I learnt to read. The mulberry tree in the yard is gone, and a car park stands where we once played marbles, but I can almost hear the bell and the chanting of tables through the open windows. How short those afternoons seemed then, and how long ago they are now. The writer's mood in this passage is:
questions.x: The writer fondly remembers the past and feels it is now far away, which is nostalgia. There is no anger at the changes, and the writer clearly cares, so 'indifferent' is wrong.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: "The thief jumped ___ the garden wall and ran away."
questions.x: 'Over' shows movement from one side to the other above something, as when jumping a wall.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "Ayesha ___ in this hospital since 2020."
questions.x: 'Since' with a starting point takes the present perfect, for an action that began in the past and continues now.

questions.q: Choose the sentence that uses inversion after 'Here' correctly.
questions.x: After 'Here' the verb comes before a noun subject ('Here comes the bus'), but not before a pronoun ('Here it comes').

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "Hamza ___ for three hours when his mother finally called him for dinner."
questions.x: An action that continued up to a moment in the past takes the past perfect continuous.

questions.q: Which of these sentences about a meal is in the active voice?
o: A delicious meal was prepared by the cook.
A delicious meal is being prepared.
The cook prepared a delicious meal.
The meal has been prepared by the cook.
questions.x: In the active voice the subject does the action; here 'the cook' does the preparing.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "I would rather ___ at home tonight than go to the crowded bazaar."
questions.x: 'Would rather' is followed by the bare infinitive.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "The doctor and the nurse ____ waiting outside the ward."
questions.x: Repeating 'the' shows two different people joined by 'and', so the subject is plural and takes 'are'.

questions.q: Choose the correct word form: "His ____ to arrive on time cost him the job."
questions.x: After the possessive 'His', a noun is needed as the subject of 'cost'. 'Failure' is the noun; the other options are verb forms.

questions.q: "Every player in the team is excellent, so the team must be excellent." Why is this belief not necessarily true?
o: Excellent players never play in teams
A team cannot be judged at all
What is true of each part is not always true of the whole
The claim attacks the players personally
questions.x: A team also depends on teamwork and planning, so excellent individuals do not guarantee an excellent team. Reasoning from parts to the whole can fail.

questions.q: Find the next number: 5, 6, 9, 15, 25, 40, ?
questions.x: The differences are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, which themselves grow by 2, 3, 4, 5. The next difference is 21, so 40 + 21 = 61.

questions.q: Find the next term: 1A, 2B, 4D, 8H, ?
questions.x: The numbers double each time, and each letter is the one at that number's position. After 8 comes 16, and the 16th letter is P.

questions.q: Village Q is 4 km north of village P. Village R is 4 km east of village Q. Village S is 4 km south of village R. Where is village S from village P?
questions.x: Going north 4 km and then south 4 km cancels out, leaving only the 4 km east step. So S is 4 km east of P.

questions.q: In a code, MILK is written as KGJI. Using the same code, how is RICE written?
questions.x: Each letter is moved two places back (M to K, I to G, L to J, K to I). So R, I, C, E become P, G, A, C.

questions.q: Statement: Wheat flour prices in a city rose sharply after some traders hoarded large stocks. Courses of action: I. People should stop eating bread. II. The government should check the traders' warehouses and act against hoarding. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Hoarding is the stated cause, so checking warehouses addresses it. Asking people to stop eating bread is impractical and does not fix the cause.

questions.q: Statement: A road accident occurred because a truck driver had been driving for 18 hours without rest. Courses of action: I. Rules limiting drivers' working hours should be enforced. II. All trucks should be banned from the roads. III. Transport companies should be checked to see that their drivers get proper rest. Which course(s) of action follow?
o: I, II and III all follow
questions.x: Enforcing limits and checking companies both target driver tiredness. Banning all trucks would stop the transport of goods and is far too extreme.

questions.q: Statement: Should students keep a daily study timetable? Argument I: Yes, a timetable helps students cover all subjects and use their time well. Argument II: No, making a timetable is boring. Which argument is strong?
o: Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
questions.x: Argument I gives a real benefit linked to the question. Finding a task boring is not a strong reason against doing it.

questions.q: Statement I: The number of road accidents on a highway fell this year. Statement II: Speed cameras were installed along the highway last year. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: Speed cameras make drivers slow down, which lowers accidents. The cameras came first and are the cause, even though they are stated second.
